sections.h2: What sets a New York City sale apart
sections.html:
The city is five boroughs and five counties, so the recording office and the paperwork depend on where the house stands. Manhattan is New York County, Brooklyn is Kings County, Queens and the Bronx share names with their counties, and Staten Island is Richmond County.

The Department of Finance sorts every property into one of four tax classes by use. A house of up to three units falls in Class 1, and co-ops and most condominiums go in Class 2. The city also runs its own transfer tax on top of the state's. This page concentrates on houses rather than co-op shares.

sections.h2: Who owns homes in the city
sections.html:
Fewer than a third of households own. Owners are 32.8 percent of the 3,334,088 households, a typical owned home is valued at $777,600 and a typical rent is $1,821. Population is 8,584,629, down 2.5 percent from 2020, and workers spend 40.3 minutes getting to their jobs.

In a renter-heavy city, houses are a modest slice of the market, and the boroughs behave differently. Staten Island is the most suburban. The Bronx is the only borough on the mainland. Queens is the largest by area, Brooklyn has the most residents, and Manhattan is the smallest and densest. If your house sits near a subway stop or commuter rail line, lead the listing with that.

sections.h2: Property tax classes and due dates
sections.html:
Each tax year runs July 1 through June 30, and a bill reflects the property's tax class and assessed value. A property assessed at $250,000 or less is billed four times a year, and one above that is billed twice.

New York City tax classes and rates for tax year 2026
Tax classWhat it coversRate for tax year 2026
Class 1Most residential property of up to three units19.843%
Class 2Other primarily residential property, such as co-ops and condos12.439%
Class 3Property with gas, telephone or electric company equipment11.108%
Class 4All other property, such as offices and warehouses10.848%

Quarterly bills come due on the first of July, October, January and April, each with a grace period to the 15th. Twice-a-year bills fall on July 1 and January 1. Paying the whole year by the July due date earns a 0.50 percent discount, and interest on late balances compounds daily. If a bill is still open when you sell, ask your closing attorney how it will be handled at closing.

The NYC Tax Commission, an independent agency, takes the appeal. A Class 1 owner must file by March 15, while Classes 2, 3 and 4 face March 1, and late filings are denied. The Commission can lower an assessment, change the tax class and adjust exemptions.

Finance runs a separate track: a Request for Review to correct a description or clerical slip, due March 15 for Class 1 and April 1 for other classes. It does not replace an appeal, so file both when both apply.

Owners of high-value homes that are not their primary residence face a newer surcharge. It is 0.8 percent of market value on one, two and three-family houses worth $5 million or more, climbing to 1.05 and 1.3 percent at higher values. A house used as a primary residence by the owner, a tenant or a relative is exempt.

A sale here stacks several taxes. On the seller's side sits the state base tax of $2 per $500 of price, plus a city real property transfer tax that is usually paid along with the other closing costs. For residential conveyances at $3 million or more, the state tacks on a further $1.25 per $500, also on the seller.

The buyer's side has the mansion tax at 1 percent from $1 million up, plus a supplemental tax between 0.25 and 2.9 percent once a residential price reaches $2 million. The city return, Form NYC-RPT, is created online in ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. Both parties sign it, and a late return adds 5 percent of the tax per month, capped at 25 percent.

Your attorney can quote the exact city figure, which varies with the kind of transfer and the price. A seller living outside New York State must work out the gain and pay any estimated income tax unless an exemption on Form TP-584-NYC applies.

The certificate states the legal use of a building, and nobody may lawfully occupy a structure until the Department of Buildings issues either a final certificate or a temporary one (TCO). A final certificate never expires, but the Department will not issue one while the property has open applications or open violations.

To obtain a final certificate, the Department requires:

  • Final construction, plumbing, elevator and electrical inspection sign-offs
  • A final building survey and an Owner's Cost Affidavit
  • No open applications and no open violations

Buildings put up before 1938 may not need one. A Letter of No Objection from the borough office can document their legal use. Search your address in DOB NOW to see whether a certificate is on file.

Buyers are urged to close on a final certificate, since an expired and unrenewed TCO can make a house hard to insure, sell or refinance. If you finished a basement or built an extension without closing out the job, a cash buyer taking the house as-is will price that in, so resolve or disclose it before accepting an offer.

sections.h2: Steps for a quick house sale
sections.html:
Begin by finding out which tax class and county apply, then look up your certificate of occupancy in DOB NOW. Request a payoff letter from your lender and ask your attorney which transfer tax forms your sale needs. Compare offers on what you keep after the state tax, the city tax and any open balance. A cash buyer can take a house with open items and close without an appraisal. That helps when a missing certificate or an old violation would otherwise stall a mortgage.

Allow time for the paperwork that is specific to this city. The city transfer tax return is built online in ACRIS and signed by both sides, and a late return adds 5 percent of the tax per month, so ask your attorney to file it on the closing date. If you live outside New York State, check whether you owe estimated income tax on the gain. Keep the final closing statement, the recorded deed and the tax forms together for your records.

faqs.q: On what dates do New York City property tax bills come due?
faqs.a: July 1 and January 1 for twice-a-year payers. Quarterly payers also owe on October 1 and April 1, with a grace period running to the 15th.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 tax rate for a one-family house in the city?
faqs.a: The Class 1 rate is 19.843 percent. Class 1 covers most residential property of up to three units, so a one-family house falls in it.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my house assessment?
faqs.a: Until March 15 for Class 1, filed with the NYC Tax Commission. Owners of Class 2, 3 and 4 property must file by March 1.

faqs.q: Who bears the state transfer tax in a city sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays the base $2 per $500 unless the contract says otherwise. The buyer pays the mansion tax when the price is $1 million or more.

faqs.q: Is a certificate of occupancy required to sell?
faqs.a: Not always. A house built before 1938 may lack one, and a Letter of No Objection from the Department of Buildings can show its legal use. For anything newer or altered, expect the buyer's attorney to ask.
